KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

A closed upper low continues to slowly drift north northeast
over Quebec this afternoon with a surface trough extending south 
into New Hampshire. This boundary will be focus for scattered 
showers and isolated thunderstorms this afternoon. Instability
will be limited this afternoon with SPC mesoanalysis trends 
suggesting 100 to 250 J/kg of MLCAPE of most of the area, but a
pocket of 500 J/kg will be possible over portions of the 
western Maine mountains by mid to late afternoon. Effective
shear is currently in the 40 to 50 knot range over much of the
forecast area, but should start to gradually decrease through
the afternoon as the surface trough pushes east. That being 
said, it will not take much instability for storms to produce 
some hail with the cold mid-level temperatures in place 
overhead. The latest RAP analysis suggests Donovan heights are 
anywhere from 20 kft to 23 kft across the north where the best 
environment is forecast (freezing levels are also relatively 
low) so a marginally severe hail report is not out of the 
question under the strongest storms. Gusty winds will also be 
possible given steep low-level lapse rates.

Showers and storms should dissipate rather quickly this evening
as we lose daytime heating. Another foggy night is then
possible, especially in the valleys and over the Midcoast of 
Maine.

The upper low drifts further northeast towards the Gulf of Saint
Lawrence but another surface trough will rotate down into the
region Tuesday afternoon, leading to some more
isolated/scattered showers and storms. Instability will remain
marginal and shear will be weaker so the concern for stronger
storms is a bit lower than today. Once again, showers and storms
will diminish with the loss of diurnal heating. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...
The trough axis shifts offshore Wednesday morning with 
northwesterly flow advecting drier air into the region. High 
pressure builds in at the surface so high temperatures should be
able to climb into the low 80s south of the mountains under 
mostly clear skies and downslope flow. North of the mountains it
may take a little longer to clear out so would expect the 
ceiling for temperatures to be more in the way of mid to upper 
70s. Surface return flow begins to advect moisture back into the
region Wednesday night making for a cloudier and warmer night 
with low temperatures in the mid to upper 50s south of the 
mountains, and in the low 60s right along the coast. North of 
the mountains temperatures fall into the low 50s. High pressure 
departs to the east Thursday as a trough begins to approach from
the Great Lakes Region. Most of the day looks to remain dry 
with partly cloudy skies as southwesterly flow continues. 
Temperture-wise Thursday looks a few degrees warmer than 
Wednesday, but the difference will be felt as dewpoints climb 
into the mid-60s south of the mountains.

Looking at the tail end of the 24.12Z NAM and RRFS, the bulk of
the precipitation looks to hold off until the evening hours 
Thursday with a chance for some earlier afternoon showers in New
Hampshire as the warm front approaches. The main show looks to 
come ahead of the cold front Thursday night into Friday. NBM 
probabilities of greater than a half inch rainfall have already 
trended down since yesterday with most of the area being given a
20 to 40 percent chance. However, this may be owing to the hi-
res models starting to be ingested and depicting the more 
convective nature where higher rainfall totals will be isolated.
Speaking of convection CSU's machine learning model does have 
some low probabilities of severe weather for this period, but 
around here if the cold front is coming through too late or too
early it does so without much fanfare. Trends will continue to 
be monitored and we should be able to start fleshing out these 
details better with consecutive runs of the CAMs. 
  
The aforementioned series of fronts is progged to be through 
the area by Saturday morning, and with broad troughing 
remaining over the region temperatures remain seasonable. High 
pressure slides eastward from the Great Lakes Region through the
weekend keeping us dry despite an upper level trough. Global 
models suggest forcing from an upper level low sinking southward
out of Quebec may reach our region Sunday night into next 
Monday, but at this time range there is still much uncertainty. 
I am fine with the NBM throwing low chance PoPs into that time 
window for now, but I would not be surprised if this eventually 
changes.
